title: Reeds, homemade pads and the broken key at the funeral
summary: Lorenzo preferred hard reeds he trimmed himself and carried a needle and thread to make pads; Tio tells how a broken key at a funeral turned into a trill that moved the crowd.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I suppose they were Saturday night, wasn't it? Yeah. I wondered if you ever knew about what strength of reed Lorenzo would use. Would he use a medium or a hard, a soft reed?

Well, I think that his reed on his instrument was mostly a hard reed because when he'd buy a reed out of the stove, he'd eventually always stick it to his mouthpiece and try it out. And he'd loosen the clip and stick another old reed underneath it and probably eat it, sand it down to the end and then take that clip off and then cut that reed. That would give it a stiffer pitch.
In other words, he'd make them to suit himself a little. Suit yourself.
So, it's according to the tone that he liked. If he had the tone, the pitch that he wanted, he had it at that. If he didn't like it, well, he'd cut it some more.

In better words, he used to carry a scissor and a needle and a tread and his pocket just like a tailor. Now, that seemed foolish, but that isn't. You see, when he was coming up, we had to learn how to make pads. He doesn't like the day that you had to buy pads. You can buy pads. We had pads that you had to get your cotton. You had to get the cotton and then you had to go to work and get some kid gloves or something of that kind, some light kids. You just cut the...put the key on top of that. And then take the print of the key, take your scissors and cut it around. Get your piece of cotton. Put it in there. Get your needle and stitch it all around and make your arm. And then get yourself some rod. Get your little candle and put it on top there and then melt that rod in there and then take this pad and press this pad and... You know, you're making your own key. You're making your own pad and your own carinet. You didn't have that. Today you can go down there and buy and make the pad you want. You didn't have that. You had to make your own pad. Well, of course, you could send your carinet to World Lines or Grunwald and them did and they'd pad it for you all right. They'd send to the manufacturer and get the pad, but then it cost you money. They all know how to make your own pad. That's the reason why I tell you, you used to do like a tailor, carry your needle and tread. I remember a slip. It was in the St. Louis Cemetery right down Denville and Claiborne. There was a funeral and my brother was playing, Nero my God to be. He broke a string in one of his keys. And he took a rubber band quick out of his pocket and stuck a rubber band on that thing and he trilled it. And they had the people in there that thought that was the greatest thing in the world. One of the greatest that was played. They never heard Nero my God to be played like it was played then. Well, that wasn't but a broken key. That's wrong time. You understand? That was a misfortune, but then it sounded good.
When he got that particular note he had to thrill it to make it sound like that.

And the people thought it was great. Thought that he had it or something, you know. Hey, they congratulate on it. And he turned around and he said, I wonder what they tell him to congratulate me about it. One woman said, young man, she said, you really didn't play that in your room? I got to be. And then after that I realized, I said, what happened? He said, I don't know you. I said, I noticed you took your clarinet down. He said, yeah, I took it down. I broke a spring underneath the key. And I said, that's what the woman must have been hollering about. He said, well, I had to do something. He said, you know, to finish that number.
